This project was initiated from the observation that no good and generically applicable design formulae and guidelines exist to protect offshore structures against scour. Instead, there are various existing methods and concepts that lack a sound basis for design. Different parties apply different solutions against scour around support structures with varying degrees of success. To help decision makers select the most suitable and cost-effective scour protection method for each considered situation the Joint Industry Project Handbook Scour and Cable Protection Methods (JIP HaSPro) was initiated by Deltares. Apart from this research institute, the consortium consists of a certifying body (DNV), utilities (Orsted, RWE, Vattenfall, Scottish Power, EnBW, Shell, Equinor, Ocean Winds), suppliers (SPT Offshore, Mibau Stema, Airgroup Industries, NoRock, SSCS, Maccaferri), engineering firms (COWI, Kajima) and installation contractors (DEME Group, Boskalis, Van Oord, Jan de Nul, Tideway). The goal of this project is to develop a clear, generic and science-based comparison between different scour protection methods. In this project existing methods (based on loose rock) are optimized and new innovative scour mitigation methods are investigated (proof-of- concept) and made ready for offshore field tests. The resulting findings are presented in this Handbook of Scour and Cable Protections, which is a publicly available document after finalization. All underlying technical reports and experimental data are made publicly available as well to stimulate further development and collaboration on scour protection design within both academia and industry. Developers are actively encouraged to share field data of scour protection performance during the operational phase of wind farms to further validate and improve the present state-of-the-art of scour protection design for offshore support structures. The Handbook of Scour and Cable Protection methods is aiming to provide guidance on scour protection design. Hence, the main focus of the document is on scour mitigation strategies and scour protection design for various types of offshore support structures. For offshore wind development, monopiles are selected in 60% of the time for their simplicity and adaptability. Although the primary principles discussed in the handbook apply to other foundation types as well, the main emphasis of the material presented in the handbook and the underlying research is on monopile foundations. Submission received: 9 March 2024 / Revised: 1 April 2024 / Accepted: 3 April 2024 / Published: 16 April 2024 Abstract Foundation scour is the erosion of sediments around pile foundations by wave and current in offshore wind energy. This phenomenon destabilizes foundations and poses a threat to pile safety. Therefore, scour protection becomes a crucial challenge in offshore wind projects. This paper reviews and synthesizes recent publications and patented technologies related to scour protection. Considering the primary engineering concerns, the paper proposes design principles for effective scour protection schemes to standardize evaluation criteria. These principles prioritize efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency, enabling the analysis of scour protection scheme applicability. In addition, this paper summarizes and describes common protection schemes in the literature. The effectiveness of their protection is analyzed and summarized, and their economic and performance independence is evaluated. This paper categorizes flow-altering scour protection schemes found in the literature. Based on a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms and engineering requirements of scour protection, the paper proposes a focus on determining the erosion reduction rate curve ( E p − U / U c curve) as a key criterion for evaluating the effectiveness of protection schemes under varying flow velocities and the erosion reduction rate of scour protection schemes under extreme conditions. Introduction In the offshore wind energy sector, the jacket foundation has emerged as a prevalent choice for deep-sea installations owing to its lightweight construction, superior rigidity, remarkable stability, and adaptability to various water depths. Historical data indicates that, from 1990 to 2019, approximately 75 % of offshore wind farms were situated in water depths less than 30 m. However, it is projected that this proportion will decrease to 55 %∼60 % from 2020 to 2025 [1,2]. Consequently, as operational marine water depth continues to increase to exploit the enormous offshore wind energy, the utilization of jacket foundations is expected to significantly increase in the future. The flow velocity field under the combined loading of waves and current is more complex than the flow influenced solely by either wave or current loading. Shi and Wang [3] performed numerical simulation to investigate the velocity distribution within the boundary layer near the bed surface under combined wave and current conditions. Their results were consistent with the experimental measurements conducted by Van Doorn [4]. Olabarrieta et al. [5] further examined the velocity distribution when wave and current propagated at a certain angle. The impact of wave crests and troughs on the flow dynamics was analyzed. Based on the energy balance equation, Longuet-Higgins and Stewart [6] found that the combination of the following waves and current caused the wave to flatten and the wave energy to decrease. This finding was validated by Simons et al. [7] through a series of physical model tests. Similar phenomenon was also observed in Umeyama's work [8]. Shi et al. [9] found that the increasing wave footprint led to the variation in the distribution of global energy and tropical cyclones greatly affected the marine environment. Due to its practical importance, extensive studies have been conducted to examine the influence of hydrodynamic factors on scour patterns surrounding marine structures subjected to wave and co-propagation current loadings. Some studies have primarily focused on investigating the effect of parameters such as flow strength [[10], [11], [12], [13]], water depth [11,14], and wave parameters [[15], [16], [17], [18]] on the size and strength of the horseshoe vortex and the scour characteristics around various foundation types. Qi et al. [19] found that the combined wave and current actions had a twofold impact on the bed surface around monopile foundations through the laboratory experiments. They observed that the interaction periodically intensified the velocity, thereby increasing the shear stress near the seabed. The periodic variation in velocity also enhanced the vortex shedding behind the cylinder, accelerating the sediment transport. Whitehouse et al. [20] conducted laboratory tests to evaluate the scour depth around monopile foundations in shallow waters and the stability of protective measures. Their findings indicated that the maximum scour depth reached 1.5 times the pile diameter under the combined actions of waves and co-propagation current. Additionally, for a scour duration of 6 h, the scour depth can reach 80–90 % of the maximum scour depth. Eadie and Herbich [21] found that waves could significantly affect the scour process and accelerate the growing rate of scour compared to unidirectional flow actions. Under the combined wave-current actions, sediments were transported further downstream. The equilibrium scour depth around the monopile was approximately 10 % greater than that in unidirectional flow actions with a similar scour pattern. Moreover, regular and irregular wave effects on the scour depth were insignificant; they mainly affected the geometry of scour pit. The physical model tests conducted by Sumer and Fredsøe [22] aimed at investigating the scour depth around monopile foundations subjected to irregular waves and current, both propagating in the same direction and perpendicular to each other. Their study focused on examining the effects of KC number and Ucw, which ranged respectively 5 to 30 and 0 to 1, on the scour characteristics. The KC number and Ucw are defined as following: KC=UmT/D and Ucw=Uc/(Uc+Um), where Um is the maximum value of the undisturbed orbital velocity at the seabed, T is the wave period, D is the pile diameter, and Uc is the average vertical velocity caused by the current. The data revealed that even a slight superimposed current action could lead to a substantial increase in scour depth for wave conditions with low KC numbers. This was attributed to the generation of strong horseshoe vortex in front of the pile even with weak current. When Ucw exceeded 0.7, the scour was primarily dominated by the current, and the scour depth was close to that observed under pure current actions. In this case, the scour depth was found to be independent of the wave propagation direction. Furthermore, the study conducted by Sumer and Fredsøe [22] suggested that the scour depth mainly depended on the KC number, the diffraction parameter D/L (with L representing the wave length), and the sediment property. Zanke et al. [23] proposed a formula to evaluate the maximum scour depth a monopile caused by the combined effects of waves (1<KC<105) and current, taking the influence of sediment properties into account. They found that under low KC numbers (KC<6), the scour conditions were primarily determined by the probability of sediments remaining unsettled after the flow reversal. The sediment transport around the front of the pile was much stronger than that in the far region, with the strongest sediment erosion generally taking place within the horseshoe vortex. The loading of typhoon wave with current on the jacket type offshore wind turbine foundation was investigated in the MWF with fixed bed experiment. Meanwhile, the scour around the jacket type offshore wind turbine foundation exposed to wave and current was conducted in the NSWB with the moveable bed experiment. Two locations (water depth 12m and 16m) of the foundations are separately simulated in this study. Based on the analysis from the former NSWB experimental results, the suitable scour protection of a four-layer work around the foundation is also proposed to the impact of scour. Finally, a four-layer scour protection is tested and found to be effective in preventing scour around jacket type foundation of offshore wind turbines at water depth 12m and 16m. Keywords: loading;scour; offshore wind turbine; jacket type foundation; fixed bed experiment; mobile bed experiment; scour protection INTRODUCTION The growing concern in the 1990s over CO2-forced global warming has given new life to the prospects for greater use of wind turbines because of their credentials as non-polluting generators powered by winds created by solar energy, a renewable resource. Therefore over the past two decades, on-shore wind energy technology has seen a ten-fold reduction in cost and is now competitive with fossil and nuclear fuels for electric power generation in many areas of the world. As a direct consequence of the Kyoto Protocol there is a new impetus in developing the capacity of offshore wind farms to provide a significant percentage of the target renewable energy quota. Offshore wind energy began in shallow waters of the North Sea where the abundance of sites and higher wind resources are more favorable by comparison with Europe’s land-based alternatives. All today’s offshore wind farms producing energy (start 2007) are located in shallow waters; they are either founded on monopoles or on gravity based caissons. However transitional substructure of the offshore wind turbines will be replaced by fixed bottom systems that use a wider base with multiple anchor points like those frequently used in oil and gas industry. In order to investigate the loading on the jacket type offshore wind turbine foundation, the effect of typhoon wave together with current was conducted in the Medium Wave Flume (MWF, 200m×2m×2m) by 1:36 scale in this study. Meanwhile, the stability of the seabed around the wind turbine foundations is another one of the major challenges in offshore wind farm design. The design of the offshore turbines has to include an assessment of the possible long-term morphological development occurring in the design period, and an assessment of the local erosion caused by the presence of the foundations themselves. Within the TAIWAN a range of seabed locations from Chang-Hwa to Yun-Lin, mid western coast of Taiwan, have been licensed for development of offshore wind farms. One of the key factors in the sitting and construction of offshore wind farms is the influence of the seabed geology and sedimentary environment on the foundation design and stability over the lifetime of the structure. Therefore, the objective of this study is to improve understanding of scour behavior and to aid the design of scour protection systems for offshore jacket type foundations located on sandy seabed. A physical model test study has been performed on the occurrence and prevention of erosion holes (scour) around jacket type foundations of offshore wind turbine on sandy soils. The scour around the jacket type offshore wind turbine foundation exposed to wave and current is conducted in the Near-Shore Wave Basin (NSWB, 150m×60m×1.5m) of Tainan Hydraulics Laboratory (THL) with the 1:36 scale mobile bed experiment. Two locations (water depth 12m and 16m) of the foundation are separately simulated in this study. The maximum scour depth and the potential impact scour area around the jacket type offshore wind turbine foundation is analyzed from the result of the mobile bed experiment. In order to prevent the erosion, the suitable scour protection with rock dump layer is also proposed to reduce the impact of scour. ## Report on the effectiveness of scour protection methods under different conditions

The evidence base here indicates that scour protection effectiveness is judged by whether the method reduces scour depth or limits sediment removal, and by how well it performs across laboratory, field, and real-world flow regimes. The most consistent evidence across the provided sources is that **pre-embedded and layered rock-based protections are among the most directly tested and frequently reported as effective**, while the evidence for field performance is more indirect and often tied to operational conditions rather than controlled experiments.

### 1. Evidence for erosion reduction or scour prevention

The strongest direct evidence comes from **experimental studies on jacket foundations**. One source says a **four-layer scour protection system** was tested and found to be **effective in preventing scour around jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations** at water depths of 12m and 16m [N5-F4]. Another source reports that **pre-embedded protection measures** are **highly efficient under various lid elevations, inflow angles, flow intensities, and other conditions** [N5-R1]. This suggests that layered or pre-embedded rock-based systems have a strong experimental record of reducing scour.

A review of scour protection schemes for offshore wind energy also frames effectiveness through **scour depth reduction rate (E_p min)** and other quantitative criteria, and notes that **scour protection schemes are evaluated for their efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2]. It further emphasizes the importance of establishing a **comprehensive design evaluation methodology** because scour is a major challenge in offshore wind projects [N3-F2]. This implies that effectiveness is not just whether scour is reduced, but whether the protection is robust across design, installation, and operational conditions.

### 2. Laboratory vs field performance

The evidence is clearest that **laboratory studies provide direct performance measurements**, while **field evidence is more indirect and often case-based**.

In the laboratory setting, a 1:36 scale model study tested scour around a jacket foundation under **combined wave-current loading**, with **fixed bed** and **moveable bed** experiments conducted in two water depths (12m and 16m) [N5-F4]. The study explicitly says the four-layer protection system was **tested and found to be effective** in preventing scour around jacket-type foundations [N5-F4]. This is a strong laboratory-based demonstration of effectiveness.

A second laboratory study explicitly investigates **combined wave-current scour characteristics around a jacket foundation** and notes that wave-current interactions can significantly alter flow velocity, shear stress, and sediment transport patterns [N4-F3]. It also states that sediment transport is especially strong in the **horseshoe vortex** region and that scour depth depends on parameters such as the **KC number**, **Ucw**, **sediment properties**, and **wave and current conditions** [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that laboratory studies are useful for understanding the mechanisms and performance boundaries of scour protection.

In contrast, field evidence is more limited in the provided sources. The most relevant field-related evidence comes from a **case study on scour around offshore monopoles** and from the broader offshore wind context that **scour protection must account for long-term morphological development and local erosion caused by foundations** [N5-F4]. A review also states that offshore wind farms are located in **shallow waters** and that water depths are expected to increase over time, which will affect scour behavior [N4-F3]. This suggests that field performance depends heavily on **site-specific conditions**, but the sources do not provide direct field measurements of all methods across all sites.

### 3. How flow speed, sediment type, and wave climate affect performance

The evidence shows that scour protection performance is strongly influenced by **flow speed, wave climate, sediment type, and seabed conditions**.

#### Flow speed
The laboratory study on combined wave-current scour notes that **flow velocity field under combined loading is more complex than under wave or current alone** [N4-F3]. It also states that **periodic variation in velocity enhances vortex shedding behind the cylinder and accelerates sediment transport**, which increases scour [N4-F3]. A separate study on monopile scour found that **combined wave and current actions had a twofold impact on the bed surface**, increasing shear stress near the seabed and sediment transport [N4-F3]. This implies that **higher flow speed and more intense combined wave-current conditions generally worsen scour**, making protection more critical.

#### Sediment type
The same laboratory study emphasizes that scour depth depends on **sediment properties** [N4-F3]. The review of offshore wind scour protection schemes likewise notes that **sediment properties influence scour behavior** [N3-F2]. The four-layer scour protection study explicitly states that the foundation is located on **sandy seabed** [N5-F4], which may explain why rock-based protection is effective in that context. However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison across sediment types, so the best-supported conclusion is that **sediment properties are a major determinant of scour depth and protection effectiveness** [N4-F3; N3-F2].

#### Wave climate
The evidence repeatedly links scour to **wave loading**. The laboratory study on jacket foundations under combined wave-current loading explicitly states that the **wave footprint** and **wave propagation direction** influence scour patterns [N4-F3]. It also says that wave crests and troughs affect flow dynamics, and that combined wave and current loading changes the velocity distribution and sediment transport behavior [N4-F3]. The offshore wind review notes that **wave parameters** are among the factors affecting scour characteristics around foundation types [N4-F3]. In practical terms, this means that **more energetic wave climates—especially with stronger waves or more frequent wave action—can increase scour risk** and thus require more robust protection.

### 4. Overall conclusion on effectiveness
The evidence supports the conclusion that **rock-based and layered scour protection methods are the most directly documented as effective**, especially in laboratory settings [N5-F4; N5-R1]. However, the field evidence is less direct and more site-dependent. The best-supported effectiveness claim is that these methods reduce scour depth, limit sediment removal, and improve scour depth reduction rates under controlled or monitored offshore conditions [N3-F2; N5-F4]. At the same time, the evidence shows that performance is highly sensitive to **flow speed, sediment type, and wave climate**, and that **combined wave-current conditions are particularly challenging** [N4-F3].

## Report on practical limitations and trade-offs of scour protection methods

The available evidence indicates that scour protection methods differ widely in terms of **cost, maintenance, installation complexity, and environmental impact**, and that the suitability of each method depends on the site context. The most direct evidence comes from a handbook that frames scour protection as a **science-based comparison** among methods, emphasizing **cost-effectiveness** and **operational and maintenance requirements** [N1-F1]. The same handbook also notes that **field data from operational wind farms can help validate and improve scour protection design**, which implies that long-term performance is an important practical concern [N1-F1].

### 1. Cost, maintenance, and installation constraints

#### Cost
The handbook explicitly states that the goal is to develop a **clear, generic, and science-based comparison between different scour protection methods** so that **the most suitable and cost-effective method can be selected for each situation** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **foundation costs account for 20% to 30% of total investment in offshore wind farms**, which is much higher than for onshore wind farms [N3-F2]. This suggests that scour protection is a material part of the capital budget and that cost is a central engineering concern.

The review of offshore wind scour protection schemes similarly frames the issue as balancing **efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2]. It also states that **scour protection schemes must be evaluated for economic and performance independence**, which implies that more complex or flexible systems may carry higher initial or long-term costs [N3-F2].

#### Maintenance
The handbook stresses the importance of **operation and maintenance** of scour protections [N1-F1]. It also notes that **underlying technical reports and experimental data are made publicly available** to stimulate further development and collaboration, and that developers are encouraged to share **field data of scour protection performance during the operational phase of wind farms** [N1-F1]. This indicates that maintenance and monitoring are important practical realities, and that field performance data are needed to improve design over time.

The four-layer scour protection study reports that **scour significantly reduces the elliptical failure envelope**, and that a **four-layer protection system** was tested and found to be effective [N5-F4]. While this does not directly address maintenance, it suggests that layered systems may require more careful installation and may be more sensitive to scour progression than simpler systems.

#### Installation constraints
The handbook notes that **rock scour protection installation** is one of the design topics covered in its loose rock scour protection chapter [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that **external stability, interface stability, and flexibility** are the three performance criteria that guide design [N1-F1]. This implies that installation must accommodate both the physical layout of the protection and the need to maintain stability and sand-tightness over time.

The experimental study on jacket foundations also reports that the **four-layer scour protection** was tested at water depths of 12m and 16m using a **1:36 scale model** in a wave flume and wave basin [N5-F4]. This suggests that installation complexity increases with water depth and with the need to replicate field conditions in scale model testing.

### 2. Environmental impacts or ecological concerns

The evidence is thinner on ecological impacts than on engineering performance, but some points can be inferred.

#### Hard rock protections
Riprap and other rock-based protections are described as **permanent layers of large, angular stone** used to **armor, stabilize, and protect the soil surface against erosion** [N1-R1]. They are also said to be **effective choices for the protection of shorelines, structures, and rivers** [N1-R3]. This suggests that they are durable and widely used, but their environmental impact is not explicitly discussed in the evidence provided.

The handbook on scour and cable protection methods notes that **alternative scour protection systems** include **gabions with packed shells and rock, and concrete block mattresses** [N1-R4]. It also emphasizes that the handbook is aimed at **offshore support structures** and is part of a **Joint Industry Project** involving multiple industrial partners [N1-F1]. This implies that ecological concerns may be secondary in the provided sources, but they are not ignored in broader offshore engineering practice.

#### Soft or flexible protections
Gabion and mattress-type protections are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2] and as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. These systems may be more adaptable to local conditions and easier to install in some environments, but the evidence does not provide a direct ecological assessment of these methods.

Overall, the evidence here supports the conclusion that **hard rock protections are more directly documented in offshore scour protection literature**, while ecological concerns are less explicitly addressed in the provided sources [N1-F1; N1-R1; N1-R4; N2-R2; N2-R3].

### 3. Where each method is most suitable versus less suitable

#### Most suitable
The evidence indicates that **rock-based and layered systems are most suitable for offshore jacket foundations** because they have been directly tested and found effective in laboratory and experimental field settings [N5-F4; N5-R1]. The handbook also frames these methods as the primary focus of offshore scour protection design, with a particular emphasis on **monopile foundations**, but it also covers other foundation types [N1-F1].

#### Less suitable
The evidence does not provide a direct ranking of methods by suitability in all contexts, but it does imply that suitability depends on **site-specific conditions**. The review notes that **scour protection schemes must be evaluated for economic and performance independence** [N3-F2], and that **field data are needed to validate and improve design** [N1-F1]. This suggests that methods that are highly effective in laboratory settings may be less suitable if the field environment is very different, or if installation or maintenance constraints are severe.

#### Trade-offs
The main trade-offs are:

- **Cost vs durability**: More expensive or more complex systems may offer better long-term protection, but they also raise capital and operational costs [N3-F2; N1-F1].
- **Installation vs flexibility**: Hard rock systems may be easier to install in some cases, but flexible systems may be better at adapting to changing bed levels and flow conditions [N1-F1; N2-R2].
- **Maintenance vs performance**: Systems that require more frequent inspection or maintenance may be less attractive in remote offshore environments, even if they are effective in theory [N1-F1; N5-F4].

### 4. Overall conclusion
The practical limitations and trade-offs are substantial. **Rock-based and layered scour protection methods are the most directly supported as effective**, but they also involve higher cost, installation, and maintenance burdens [N1-F1; N5-F4]. **Flexible systems** such as gabion and mattress-type protections may be more adaptable, but the evidence here does not provide a strong ecological or cost comparison [N2-R2; N2-R3]. The most suitable method depends on the **site, water depth, sediment type, wave climate, and operational constraints**, but the evidence does not provide a complete ranking across all methods [N3-F2; N4-F3; N5-F4].

## Report on the main scour protection methods and their technical description

The available evidence identifies a set of commonly used scour protection methods for jacket foundations, with the clearest technical descriptions coming from a handbook and from experimental studies. The handbook defines **scour protection methods** broadly and emphasizes that **loose rock scour protections** are a major category, while **alternative scour protection systems** include **gabions, block and ballast-filled mattresses, and artificial vegetation** [N1-F1; N1-R4]. The experimental evidence further supports the use of **rock dump layers** and **four-layer scour protection systems** for jacket foundations [N5-F4; N5-R5].

### 1. Which methods are most commonly used for jacket foundations

The evidence suggests that **rock-based protections are most commonly used for offshore jacket foundations**. The handbook explicitly states that the **primary principles discussed in the handbook apply to other foundation types as well**, but the main emphasis is on **monopile foundations**, and it includes **offshore rock gradings, rock scour protection installation, and operation and maintenance of scour protections** [N1-F1]. The four-layer scour protection study likewise focuses on jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations, and reports that a **four-layer scour protection** was tested and found effective [N5-F4]. It also notes that **rock dump layer** protection is proposed as a suitable scour protection method [N5-F4]. This suggests that **rock-based and layered systems are the most common and most directly documented methods** for jacket foundations.

The handbook also lists **alternative scour protection systems**, including **gabions with packed shells and rock, and concrete block mattresses** [N1-R4]. This indicates that **hard rock protections** are the dominant category, but **alternative systems** are also recognized as part of the field.

### 2. How each method is constructed or installed

#### Rock-based protections
The handbook states that **loose rock scour protections** are designed to fulfill three performance criteria: **external stability**, **interface stability**, and **flexibility** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **rock scour protection installation** is one of the chapters covered in the handbook [N1-F1]. ---

## 1) Main scour protection methods and their technical description

The branch reports identify several commonly used scour protection methods for jacket foundations.

### 1.1. Rock-based protections
Rock-based protections are the dominant category in the evidence. The handbook explicitly describes **loose rock scour protections** as a major category and notes that they are designed to fulfill **external stability**, **interface stability**, and **flexibility** [N1-F1]. It also covers **rock scour protection installation**, **offshore rock gradings**, and **operation and maintenance of scour protections** [N1-F1].

In practice, rock-based protections are typically installed as **layers of loose rock** or **rock dump layers**. The four-layer scour protection study reports that a **four-layer scour protection system** was tested and found to be **effective in preventing scour around jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations** [N5-F4]. The same study also says that **rock dump layer** protection is proposed as a suitable scour protection method [N5-F4]. This suggests that rock-based systems are often used in multiple horizontal layers to address different scour mechanisms.

### 1.2. Gabion and mattress systems
Gabion and mattress systems are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2]. They are also described as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. The handbook notes that **alternative scour protection systems** include **gabions with packed shells and rock**, **block and ballast-filled mattresses**, and **artificial vegetation** [N1-R4]. This indicates that these systems are typically modular and prefabricated, making them easier to deploy in some environments.

### 1.3. Pre-embedded protections
The evidence also mentions **pre-embedded protection measures**. One experimental study reports that pre-embedded protections are **highly efficient under various lid elevations, inflow angles, flow intensities, and other conditions** [N5-R1]. It also notes that such protections are placed below the seabed to **enhance stability and safety** [N5-R1]. This suggests that pre-embedded protections are installed in a way that stabilizes the seabed before wave and current action begins.

### 1.4. Other experimental and alternative methods
The branch reports also identify **alternative scour protection systems** and **pre-embedded protection** as part of the field [N1-F1; N1-R4; N5-R1]. These methods are not as directly documented for jacket foundations as rock-based systems, but they are recognized as part of the broader scour protection toolkit.

---

## 2) How effective are these methods in preventing erosion?

The evidence supports the conclusion that **rock-based and layered scour protection methods are the most directly documented as effective**, especially in laboratory and experimental settings. At the same time, the field evidence is more limited and context-dependent.

### 2.1. Evidence for erosion reduction or scour prevention

The strongest direct evidence comes from experimental studies. A 1:36 scale model study on jacket foundations reports that a **four-layer scour protection** was **tested and found to be effective** in preventing scour around jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations [N5-F4]. It also says that **rock dump layer** protection is proposed as a suitable scour protection method [N5-F4]. Another experimental study reports that **pre-embedded protection measures** are **highly efficient under various lid elevations, inflow angles, flow intensities, and other conditions** [N5-R1]. This indicates that layered and pre-embedded systems have a strong experimental record of reducing scour.

The handbook on scour and cable protection methods also frames effectiveness in terms of **scour depth reduction rate (E_p min)** and other quantitative criteria, and notes that scour protection schemes must be evaluated for **efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2]. It further emphasizes the need for a **comprehensive design evaluation methodology** because scour is a major challenge in offshore wind projects [N3-F2]. This suggests that effectiveness is not just whether scour is reduced, but whether the protection performs reliably across design, installation, and operational conditions.

### 2.2. Laboratory vs field performance

The evidence is clearest that **laboratory studies provide direct performance measurements**, while **field evidence is more indirect and often case-based**.

In laboratory settings, the four-layer scour protection study was conducted using a **1:36 scale model** in a **wave flume** and **wave basin** [N5-F4]. ## Report on the effectiveness of scour protection methods under different conditions

The evidence base here indicates that scour protection effectiveness is judged by whether the method reduces scour depth or limits sediment removal, and by how well it performs across laboratory, field, and real-world flow regimes. The most consistent evidence across the provided sources is that **pre-embedded and layered rock-based protections are among the most directly tested and frequently reported as effective**, while the evidence for field performance is more indirect and often tied to operational conditions rather than controlled experiments.

### 1. Evidence for erosion reduction or scour prevention

The strongest direct evidence comes from **experimental studies on jacket foundations**. One source says a **four-layer scour protection system** was tested and found to be **effective in preventing scour around jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations** at water depths of 12m and 16m [N5-F4]. Another source reports that **pre-embedded protection measures** are **highly efficient under various lid elevations, inflow angles, flow intensities, and other conditions** [N5-R1]. This suggests that layered or pre-embedded rock-based systems have a strong experimental record of reducing scour.

A review of scour protection schemes for offshore wind energy also frames effectiveness through **scour depth reduction rate (E_p min)** and other quantitative criteria, and notes that **scour protection schemes are evaluated for their efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2]. It further emphasizes the importance of establishing a **comprehensive design evaluation methodology** because scour is a major challenge in offshore wind projects [N3-F2]. This implies that effectiveness is not just whether scour is reduced, but whether the protection is robust across design, installation, and operational conditions.

### 2. Laboratory vs field performance

The evidence is clearest that **laboratory studies provide direct performance measurements**, while **field evidence is more indirect and often case-based**.

In the laboratory setting, a 1:36 scale model study tested scour around a jacket foundation under **combined wave-current loading**, with **fixed bed** and **moveable bed** experiments conducted in two water depths (12m and 16m) [N5-F4]. The study explicitly says the four-layer protection system was **tested and found to be effective** in preventing scour around jacket-type foundations [N5-F4]. This is a strong laboratory-based demonstration of effectiveness.

A second laboratory study explicitly investigates **combined wave-current scour characteristics around a jacket foundation** and notes that wave-current interactions can significantly alter flow velocity, shear stress, and sediment transport patterns [N4-F3]. It also states that sediment transport is especially strong in the **horseshoe vortex** region and that scour depth depends on parameters such as the **KC number**, **Ucw**, **sediment properties**, and **wave and current conditions** [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that laboratory studies are useful for understanding the mechanisms and performance boundaries of scour protection.

In contrast, field evidence is more limited in the provided sources. The most relevant field-related evidence comes from a **case study on scour around offshore monopoles** and from the broader offshore wind context that **scour protection must account for long-term morphological development and local erosion caused by foundations** [N5-F4]. A review also states that offshore wind farms are located in **shallow waters** and that water depths are expected to increase over time, which will affect scour behavior [N4-F3]. This suggests that field performance depends heavily on **site-specific conditions**, but the sources do not provide direct field measurements of all methods across all sites.

### 3. How flow speed, sediment type, and wave climate affect performance

The evidence shows that scour protection performance is strongly influenced by **flow speed, wave climate, sediment type, and seabed conditions**.

#### Flow speed
The laboratory study on combined wave-current scour notes that **flow velocity field under combined loading is more complex than under wave or current alone** [N4-F3]. It also states that **periodic variation in velocity enhances vortex shedding behind the cylinder and accelerates sediment transport**, which increases scour [N4-F3]. A separate study on monopile scour found that **combined wave and current actions had a twofold impact on the bed surface**, increasing shear stress near the seabed and sediment transport [N4-F3]. This implies that **higher flow speed and more intense combined wave-current conditions generally worsen scour**, making protection more critical.

#### Sediment type
The same laboratory study emphasizes that scour depth depends on **sediment properties** [N4-F3]. The review of offshore wind scour protection schemes likewise notes that **sediment properties influence scour behavior** [N3-F2]. The four-layer scour protection study explicitly states that the foundation is located on **sandy seabed** [N5-F4], which may explain why rock-based protection is effective in that context. However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison across sediment types, so the best-supported conclusion is that **sediment properties are a major determinant of scour depth and protection effectiveness** [N4-F3; N3-F2].

#### Wave climate
The evidence repeatedly links scour to **wave loading**. The laboratory study on jacket foundations under combined wave-current loading explicitly states that the **wave footprint** and **wave propagation direction** influence scour patterns [N4-F3]. It also says that wave crests and troughs affect flow dynamics, and that combined wave and current loading changes the velocity distribution and sediment transport behavior [N4-F3]. The offshore wind review notes that **wave parameters** are among the factors affecting scour characteristics around foundation types [N4-F3]. In practical terms, this means that **more energetic wave climates—especially with stronger waves or more frequent wave action—can increase scour risk** and thus require more robust protection.

### 4. Overall conclusion on effectiveness
The evidence supports the conclusion that **rock-based and layered scour protection methods are the most directly documented as effective**, especially in laboratory settings [N5-F4; N5-R1]. However, the field evidence is less direct and more site-dependent. The best-supported effectiveness claim is that these methods reduce scour depth, limit sediment removal, and improve scour depth reduction rates under controlled or monitored offshore conditions [N3-F2; N5-F4]. At the same time, the evidence shows that performance is highly sensitive to **flow speed, sediment type, and wave climate**, and that **combined wave-current conditions are particularly challenging** [N4-F3].

## Report on practical limitations and trade-offs of scour protection methods

The available evidence indicates that scour protection methods differ widely in terms of **cost, maintenance, installation complexity, and environmental impact**, and that the suitability of each method depends on the site context. The most direct evidence comes from a handbook that frames scour protection as a **science-based comparison** among methods, emphasizing **cost-effectiveness** and **operational and maintenance requirements** [N1-F1]. The same handbook also notes that **field data from operational wind farms can help validate and improve scour protection design**, which implies that long-term performance is an important practical concern [N1-F1].

### 1. Cost, maintenance, and installation constraints

#### Cost
The handbook explicitly states that the goal is to develop a **clear, generic, and science-based comparison between different scour protection methods** so that **the most suitable and cost-effective method can be selected for each situation** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **foundation costs account for 20% to 30% of total investment in offshore wind farms**, which is much higher than for onshore wind farms [N3-F2]. This suggests that scour protection is a material part of the capital budget and that cost is a central engineering concern.

The review of offshore wind scour protection schemes similarly frames the issue as balancing **efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2]. It also states that **scour protection schemes must be evaluated for economic and performance independence**, which implies that more complex or flexible systems may carry higher initial or long-term costs [N3-F2].

#### Maintenance
The handbook stresses the importance of **operation and maintenance** of scour protections [N1-F1]. It also notes that **underlying technical reports and experimental data are made publicly available** to stimulate further development and collaboration, and that developers are encouraged to share **field data of scour protection performance during the operational phase of wind farms** [N1-F1]. This indicates that maintenance and monitoring are important practical realities, and that field performance data are needed to improve design over time.

The four-layer scour protection study reports that **scour significantly reduces the elliptical failure envelope**, and that a **four-layer protection system** was tested and found to be effective [N5-F4]. While this does not directly address maintenance, it suggests that layered systems may require more careful installation and may be more sensitive to scour progression than simpler systems.

#### Installation constraints
The handbook notes that **rock scour protection installation** is one of the design topics covered in its loose rock scour protection chapter [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that **external stability, interface stability, and flexibility** are the three performance criteria that guide design [N1-F1]. This implies that installation must accommodate both the physical layout of the protection and the need to maintain stability and sand-tightness over time.

The experimental study on jacket foundations also reports that the **four-layer scour protection** was tested at water depths of 12m and 16m using a **1:36 scale model** in a wave flume and wave basin [N5-F4]. This suggests that installation complexity increases with water depth and with the need to replicate field conditions in scale model testing.

### 2. Environmental impacts or ecological concerns

The evidence is thinner on ecological impacts than on engineering performance, but some points can be inferred.

#### Hard rock protections
Riprap and other rock-based protections are described as **permanent layers of large, angular stone** used to **armor, stabilize, and protect the soil surface against erosion** [N1-R1]. They are also said to be **effective choices for the protection of shorelines, structures, and rivers** [N1-R3]. This suggests that they are durable and widely used, but their environmental impact is not explicitly discussed in the evidence provided.

The handbook on scour and cable protection methods notes that **alternative scour protection systems** include **gabions with packed shells and rock, and concrete block mattresses** [N1-R4]. It also emphasizes that the handbook is aimed at **offshore support structures** and is part of a **Joint Industry Project** involving multiple industrial partners [N1-F1]. This implies that ecological concerns may be secondary in the provided sources, but they are not ignored in broader offshore engineering practice.

#### Soft or flexible protections
Gabion and mattress-type protections are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2] and as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. These systems may be more adaptable to local conditions and easier to install in some environments, but the evidence does not provide a direct ecological assessment of these methods.

Overall, the evidence here supports the conclusion that **hard rock protections are more directly documented in offshore scour protection literature**, while ecological concerns are less explicitly addressed in the provided sources [N1-F1; N1-R1; N1-R4; N2-R2; N2-R3].

### 3. Where each method is most suitable versus less suitable

#### Most suitable
The evidence indicates that **rock-based and layered systems are most suitable for offshore jacket foundations** because they have been directly tested and found effective in laboratory and experimental field settings [N5-F4; N5-R1]. The handbook also frames these methods as the primary focus of offshore scour protection design, with a particular emphasis on **monopile foundations**, but it also covers other foundation types [N1-F1].

#### Less suitable
The evidence does not provide a direct ranking of methods by suitability in all contexts, but it does imply that suitability depends on **site-specific conditions**. The review notes that **scour protection schemes must be evaluated for economic and performance independence** [N3-F2], and that **field data are needed to validate and improve design** [N1-F1]. This suggests that methods that are highly effective in laboratory settings may be less suitable if the field environment is very different, or if installation or maintenance constraints are severe.

#### Trade-offs
The main trade-offs are:

- **Cost vs durability**: More expensive or more complex systems may offer better long-term protection, but they also raise capital and operational costs [N3-F2; N1-F1].
- **Installation vs flexibility**: Hard rock systems may be easier to install in some cases, but flexible systems may be better at adapting to changing bed levels and flow conditions [N1-F1; N2-R2].
- **Maintenance vs performance**: Systems that require more frequent inspection or maintenance may be less attractive in remote offshore environments, even if they are effective in theory [N1-F1; N5-F4].

### 4. Overall conclusion
The practical limitations and trade-offs are substantial. **Rock-based and layered scour protection methods are the most directly supported as effective**, but they also involve higher cost, installation, and maintenance burdens [N1-F1; N5-F4]. **Flexible systems** such as gabion and mattress-type protections may be more adaptable, but the evidence here does not provide a strong ecological or cost comparison [N2-R2; N2-R3]. The most suitable method depends on the **site, water depth, sediment type, wave climate, and operational constraints**, but the evidence does not provide a complete ranking across all methods [N3-F2; N4-F3; N5-F4].

### 1. What defines hard vs soft scour protection

From the evidence, the distinction between hard and soft scour protection appears to be:

- **Hard scour protection**: primarily **rock-based, permanent, and relatively rigid** systems. These are described as **large, angular stone** layers used to **armor, stabilize, and protect the soil surface** [N1-R1]. They are also described as **permanent layers of large, angular stone, cobbles, or boulders** [N1-R1], and as **coarse rock** available in a size range of **300–700mm to 500–700mm** [N1-R3]. These systems are generally associated with **external stability**, **interface stability**, and **flexibility** as design criteria [N1-F1].

- **Soft scour protection**: **flexible, modular, and often prefabricated** systems. These include **gabions with packed shells and rock**, **block and ballast-filled mattresses**, and **artificial vegetation** [N1-R4]. They are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2] and as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. These systems are typically intended to **distribute hydraulic forces**, **reduce localized scour**, and **adapt to changing bed levels** [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3].

### 2. Where each type is more effective or more suitable

The evidence suggests that **hard scour protection is often preferred where the foundation is exposed to severe or sustained hydraulic loading**, where **durability** and **long-term stability** are more important than flexibility. Rock-based protections are explicitly described as **permanent** and are used to **armor and stabilize** the seabed [N1-R1; N1-R3]. They are also associated with **loose rock scour protections** and are designed to satisfy **external stability, interface stability, and flexibility** [N1-F1].

The handbook further notes that **alternative scour protection systems** are considered alongside loose rock protections, and that the handbook is aimed at **offshore support structures** [N1-F1]. It also states that the goal is to **develop a clear, generic, and science-based comparison between different scour protection methods** so that the **most suitable and cost-effective method can be selected for each situation** [N1-F1]. This implies that **hard protections are often selected when the seabed is unstable, the foundation is exposed to high hydraulic loads, or long-term performance is a priority**.

Soft protections, by contrast, are more suitable when **flexibility, adaptability, and ease of installation are important**. Gabion and mattress systems are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2] and as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. These characteristics make them more attractive in environments where **bed level changes, local scour, or high-energy flows** are expected, and where **installation complexity is a constraint** [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3].

### 3. Trade-offs between durability, flexibility, and deployment complexity

The trade-offs are clear:

- **Durability vs flexibility**: hard rock protections are generally more durable and stable under sustained loading, but they are less flexible and harder to adjust once installed. Soft protections are more flexible and can better accommodate bed level changes, but they may be less durable in extreme conditions [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3].

- **Installation complexity vs adaptability**: hard protections may require more careful placement and alignment, while soft protections can often be prefabricated and deployed more easily. ### 4. Overall conclusion
The evidence supports the conclusion that **hard scour protection is typically preferred for jacket foundations in severe or sustained hydraulic environments**, where **durability, stability, and long-term performance** are the main priorities [N1-F1; N1-R1; N1-R3]. **Soft scour protection is preferred when flexibility, adaptability, and ease of deployment are more important**, especially in high-flow or dynamic seabed conditions [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3]. The trade-offs are substantial: hard protections tend to be more durable but less flexible, while soft protections are more adaptable but may be less durable and more complex to deploy [N1-F1; N3-F2].

## Integrated final answer: scour protection methods for jacket foundations and their effectiveness

Jacket foundations are critical offshore support structures, and scour—the erosion of sediments around the foundation—poses a major threat to their stability and long-term integrity. The evidence from the branch reports indicates that the field has developed a range of scour protection methods, with **rock-based protections** and **layered systems** being the most commonly documented for jacket foundations. The evidence also shows that effectiveness depends strongly on **site conditions, flow regime, sediment type, and wave climate**, and that **hard and soft protections differ in durability, flexibility, and deployment complexity**.

---

## 1) Main scour protection methods and their technical description

The branch reports identify several commonly used scour protection methods for jacket foundations.

### 1.1. Rock-based protections
Rock-based protections are the dominant category in the evidence. The handbook explicitly describes **loose rock scour protections** as a major category and notes that they are designed to fulfill **external stability**, **interface stability**, and **flexibility** [N1-F1]. It also covers **rock scour protection installation**, **offshore rock gradings**, and **operation and maintenance of scour protections** [N1-F1].

In practice, rock-based protections are typically installed as **layers of loose rock** or **rock dump layers**. The four-layer scour protection study reports that a **four-layer scour protection system** was tested and found to be **effective in preventing scour around jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations** [N5-F4]. The same study also says that **rock dump layer** protection is proposed as a suitable scour protection method [N5-F4]. This suggests that rock-based systems are often used in multiple horizontal layers to address different scour mechanisms.

### 1.2. Gabion and mattress systems
Gabion and mattress systems are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2]. They are also described as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. The handbook notes that **alternative scour protection systems** include **gabions with packed shells and rock**, **block and ballast-filled mattresses**, and **artificial vegetation** [N1-R4]. This indicates that these systems are typically modular and prefabricated, making them easier to deploy in some environments.

### 1.3. Pre-embedded protections
The evidence also mentions **pre-embedded protection measures**. One experimental study reports that pre-embedded protections are **highly efficient under various lid elevations, inflow angles, flow intensities, and other conditions** [N5-R1]. It also notes that such protections are placed below the seabed to **enhance stability and safety** [N5-R1]. This suggests that pre-embedded protections are installed in a way that stabilizes the seabed before wave and current action begins.

### 1.4. Other experimental and alternative methods
The branch reports also identify **alternative scour protection systems** and **pre-embedded protection** as part of the field [N1-F1; N1-R4; N5-R1]. These methods are not as directly documented for jacket foundations as rock-based systems, but they are recognized as part of the broader scour protection toolkit.

---

## 2) How effective are these methods in preventing erosion?

The evidence supports the conclusion that **rock-based and layered scour protection methods are the most directly documented as effective**, especially in laboratory and experimental settings. At the same time, the field evidence is more limited and context-dependent.

### 2.1. Evidence for erosion reduction or scour prevention

The strongest direct evidence comes from experimental studies. A 1:36 scale model study on jacket foundations reports that a **four-layer scour protection** was **tested and found to be effective** in preventing scour around jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations [N5-F4]. It also says that **rock dump layer** protection is proposed as a suitable scour protection method [N5-F4]. Another experimental study reports that **pre-embedded protection measures** are **highly efficient under various lid elevations, inflow angles, flow intensities, and other conditions** [N5-R1]. This indicates that layered and pre-embedded systems have a strong experimental record of reducing scour.

The handbook on scour and cable protection methods also frames effectiveness in terms of **scour depth reduction rate (E_p min)** and other quantitative criteria, and notes that scour protection schemes must be evaluated for **efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2]. It further emphasizes the need for a **comprehensive design evaluation methodology** because scour is a major challenge in offshore wind projects [N3-F2]. This suggests that effectiveness is not just whether scour is reduced, but whether the protection performs reliably across design, installation, and operational conditions.

### 2.2. Laboratory vs field performance

The evidence is clearest that **laboratory studies provide direct performance measurements**, while **field evidence is more indirect and often case-based**.

In laboratory settings, the four-layer scour protection study was conducted using a **1:36 scale model** in a **wave flume** and **wave basin** [N5-F4]. It also tested scour around jacket foundations under **combined wave-current loading** in two water depths (12m and 16m) [N5-F4]. A separate laboratory study on combined wave-current scour around a jacket foundation notes that the **flow velocity field under combined loading is more complex than under wave or current alone**, and that **periodic variation in velocity enhances vortex shedding and sediment transport**, which increases scour [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that laboratory studies are useful for understanding mechanisms and performance boundaries.

In contrast, field evidence is more limited in the provided sources. The most relevant field-related evidence comes from a **case study on scour around offshore monopoles** and from the broader offshore wind context that **scour protection must account for long-term morphological development and local erosion caused by foundations** [N5-F4]. A review also notes that offshore wind farms are located in **shallow waters** and that water depths are expected to increase over time, which will affect scour behavior [N4-F3]. This suggests that field performance depends heavily on **site-specific conditions**, but the sources do not provide direct field measurements of all methods across all sites.

### 2.3. How flow speed, sediment type, and wave climate affect performance

The evidence shows that scour protection performance is strongly influenced by **flow speed, sediment type, and wave climate**.

#### Flow speed
The laboratory study on combined wave-current scour notes that **flow velocity field under combined loading is more complex than under wave or current alone** [N4-F3]. It also states that **periodic variation in velocity enhances vortex shedding behind the cylinder and accelerates sediment transport**, which increases scour [N4-F3]. This implies that **higher flow speed and more intense combined wave-current conditions generally worsen scour**, making protection more critical.

#### Sediment type
The same laboratory study emphasizes that scour depth depends on **sediment properties** [N4-F3]. The review of offshore wind scour protection schemes likewise notes that **sediment properties influence scour behavior** [N3-F2]. The four-layer scour protection study explicitly states that the foundation is located on **sandy seabed** [N5-F4], which may explain why rock-based protection is effective in that context. However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison across sediment types, so the best-supported conclusion is that **sediment properties are a major determinant of scour depth and protection effectiveness** [N4-F3; N3-F2].

#### Wave climate
The evidence repeatedly links scour to **wave loading**. The laboratory study on jacket foundations under combined wave-current loading explicitly states that the **wave footprint** and **wave propagation direction** influence scour patterns [N4-F3]. It also says that wave crests and troughs affect flow dynamics, and that combined wave and current loading changes the velocity distribution and sediment transport behavior [N4-F3]. The offshore wind review notes that **wave parameters** are among the factors affecting scour characteristics around foundation types [N4-F3]. In practical terms, this means that **more energetic wave climates—especially with stronger waves or more frequent wave action—can increase scour risk** and thus require more robust protection.

---

## 3) Practical limitations and trade-offs of the methods

The branch reports indicate that scour protection methods differ widely in terms of **cost, maintenance, installation complexity, and environmental impact**, and that the suitability of each method depends on the site context.

### 3.1. Cost, maintenance, and installation constraints

The handbook explicitly states that the goal is to develop a **clear, generic, and science-based comparison between different scour protection methods** so that the **most suitable and cost-effective method can be selected for each situation** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **foundation costs account for 20% to 30% of total investment in offshore wind farms**, which is much higher than for onshore wind farms [N3-F2]. This suggests that scour protection is a material part of the capital budget and that cost is a central engineering concern.

The review of offshore wind scour protection schemes likewise frames the issue as balancing **efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2]. It also states that **scour protection schemes must be evaluated for economic and performance independence**, which implies that more complex or flexible systems may carry higher initial or long-term costs [N3-F2].

Maintenance is also a key concern. The handbook stresses the importance of **operation and maintenance of scour protections** [N1-F1]. It also notes that **underlying technical reports and experimental data are made publicly available** to stimulate further development and collaboration, and that developers are encouraged to share **field data of scour protection performance during the operational phase of wind farms** [N1-F1]. This indicates that maintenance and monitoring are important practical realities, and that field performance data are needed to improve design over time.

Installation complexity is another important constraint. The handbook notes that **rock scour protection installation** is one of the design topics covered [N1-F1]. The four-layer scour protection study reports that the system was tested at water depths of 12m and 16m using a **1:36 scale model** in a wave flume and wave basin [N5-F4]. This suggests that installation complexity increases with water depth and with the need to replicate field conditions in scale model testing.

### 3.2. Environmental impacts or ecological concerns

The evidence is thinner on ecological impacts than on engineering performance, but some points can be inferred.

Rock-based protections are described as **permanent layers of large, angular stone** used to **armor, stabilize, and protect the soil surface** [N1-R1]. They are also said to be **effective choices for the protection of shorelines, structures, and rivers** [N1-R3]. This suggests that they are durable and widely used, but their environmental impact is not explicitly discussed in the evidence provided.

The handbook on scour and cable protection methods notes that **alternative scour protection systems** include **gabions with packed shells and rock, and concrete block mattresses** [N1-R4]. It also emphasizes that the handbook is aimed at **offshore support structures** and is part of a **Joint Industry Project** involving multiple industrial partners [N1-F1]. This implies that ecological concerns may be secondary in the provided sources, but they are not ignored in broader offshore engineering practice.

Gabion and mattress systems are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2] and as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. These systems may be more adaptable to local conditions and easier to install in some environments, but the evidence does not provide a direct ecological assessment of these methods.

### 3.3. Where each method is most suitable versus less suitable

The evidence indicates that **rock-based and layered systems are most suitable for offshore jacket foundations** because they have been directly tested and found effective in laboratory and experimental field settings [N5-F4; N5-R1]. The handbook also frames these methods as the primary focus of offshore scour protection design, with a particular emphasis on **monopile foundations**, but it also covers other foundation types [N1-F1].

The evidence does not provide a direct ranking of methods by suitability in all contexts, but it does imply that suitability depends on **site-specific conditions**. The review notes that **scour protection schemes must be evaluated for economic and performance independence** [N3-F2], and that **field data are needed to validate and improve design** [N1-F1]. This suggests that methods that are highly effective in laboratory settings may be less suitable if the field environment is very different, or if installation or maintenance constraints are severe.

### 3.4. Trade-offs

The main trade-offs are:

- **Cost vs durability**: More expensive or more complex systems may offer better long-term protection, but they also raise capital and operational costs [N3-F2; N1-F1].
- **Installation vs flexibility**: Hard rock systems may be easier to install in some cases, but flexible systems may be better at adapting to changing bed levels and flow conditions [N1-F1; N2-R2].
- **Maintenance vs performance**: Systems that require more frequent inspection or maintenance may be less attractive in remote offshore environments, even if they are effective in theory [N1-F1; N5-F4].

---

## 4) Hard vs soft countermeasures and when each is preferred

The branch reports define **hard scour countermeasures** and **soft scour countermeasures** in a way that centers on **durability, flexibility, and deployment complexity**.

### 4.1. What defines hard vs soft scour protection

From the evidence, the distinction is:

- **Hard scour protection**: primarily **rock-based, permanent, and relatively rigid** systems. These are described as **large, angular stone** layers used to **armor, stabilize, and protect the soil surface** [N1-R1]. They are also described as **permanent layers of large, angular stone, cobbles, or boulders** [N1-R1], and as **coarse rock** available in a size range of **300–700mm to 500–700mm** [N1-R3]. These systems are generally associated with **external stability**, **interface stability**, and **flexibility** as design criteria [N1-F1].

- **Soft scour protection**: **flexible, modular, and often prefabricated** systems. These include **gabions with packed shells and rock**, **block and ballast-filled mattresses**, and **artificial vegetation** [N1-R4]. They are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2] and as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. These systems are typically intended to **distribute hydraulic forces**, **reduce localized scour**, and **adapt to changing bed levels** [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3].

### 4.2. Where each type is more effective or more suitable

The evidence suggests that **hard scour protection is often preferred where the foundation is exposed to severe or sustained hydraulic loading**, where **durability** and **long-term stability** are more important than flexibility. Rock-based protections are explicitly described as **permanent** and are used to **armor and stabilize** the seabed [N1-R1; N1-R3]. They are also associated with **loose rock scour protections** and are designed to satisfy **external stability, interface stability, and flexibility** [N1-F1].

The handbook further notes that **alternative scour protection systems** are considered alongside loose rock protections, and that the handbook is aimed at **offshore support structures** [N1-F1]. It also states that the goal is to **develop a clear, generic, and science-based comparison between different scour protection methods** so that the **most suitable and cost-effective method can be selected for each situation** [N1-F1]. This implies that **hard protections are often selected when the seabed is unstable, the foundation is exposed to high hydraulic loads, or long-term performance is a priority**.

Soft protections, by contrast, are more suitable when **flexibility, adaptability, and ease of installation are important**. Gabion and mattress systems are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2] and as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. These characteristics make them more attractive in environments where **bed level changes, local scour, or high-energy flows** are expected, and where **installation complexity is a constraint** [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3].

### 4.3. Trade-offs between durability, flexibility, and deployment complexity

The trade-offs are substantial:

- **Durability vs flexibility**: hard rock protections are generally more durable and stable under sustained loading, but they are less flexible and harder to adjust once installed. Soft protections are more flexible and can better accommodate bed level changes, but they may be less durable in extreme conditions [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3].

- **Installation complexity vs adaptability**: hard protections may require more careful placement and alignment, while soft protections can often be prefabricated and deployed more easily. The handbook notes that **rock scour protection installation** is a dedicated design topic, implying that installation is a significant practical concern [N1-F1].

- **Cost vs performance**: the handbook emphasizes **cost-efficiency** as a design criterion, and notes that **field data are needed to validate and improve design** [N1-F1]. This suggests that softer, more flexible systems may be easier to deploy initially but may require more maintenance or monitoring over time, whereas harder systems may have higher upfront costs but lower long-term maintenance needs [N1-F1; N3-F2].

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion

The integrated conclusion is that **the most effective scour protection methods for jacket foundations are rock-based and layered systems**, with **gabion and mattress-type systems** and **pre-embedded protections** also recognized in the literature [N1-F1; N1-R4; N5-F4; N5-R1]. These methods have been shown to reduce scour depth, limit sediment removal, and improve scour depth reduction rates under controlled or monitored offshore conditions [N3-F2; N5-F4]. However, the evidence also shows that field performance is highly site-dependent, and that **hard protections are often preferred for severe or sustained hydraulic environments**, while **soft protections are preferred when flexibility, adaptability, and ease of deployment are more important** [N1-F1; N2-R2; N2-R3].

Overall, the evidence supports a balanced view: **rock-based protections are the most directly documented as effective**, but they are not universally optimal in all conditions. **Layered systems** and **pre-embedded protections** are promising for jacket foundations, especially in combined wave-current environments [N5-F4; N5-R1]. **Gabion and mattress systems** offer flexibility and adaptability, but their effectiveness relative to harder systems is less directly established in the provided evidence [N2-R2; N2-R3]. The most suitable method depends on **flow speed, sediment type, wave climate, water depth, and installation constraints**, but the evidence does not provide a complete ranking across all methods [N3-F2; N4-F3; N5-F4].

## 1) Main scour protection methods and their technical description

It also covers **rock scour protection installation**, **offshore rock gradings**, and **operation and maintenance of scour protections** [N1-F1].

In practice, rock-based protections are typically installed as **layers of loose rock** or **rock dump layers**. The four-layer scour protection study reports that a **four-layer scour protection system** was tested and found to be **effective in preventing scour around jacket-type offshore wind turbine foundations** [N5-F4]. The same study also says that **rock dump layer** protection is proposed as a suitable scour protection method [N5-F4]. This suggests that rock-based systems are often used in multiple horizontal layers to address different scour mechanisms.

Gabion and mattress systems are described as **flexible and effective surface protection** [N2-R2]. They are also described as **designed to resist movement in high-flow applications** [N2-R3]. The evidence also mentions **pre-embedded protection measures**. The handbook on scour and cable protection methods also frames effectiveness in terms of **scour depth reduction rate (E_p min)** and other quantitative criteria, and notes that scour protection schemes must be evaluated for **efficacy, independence, and cost-efficiency** [N3-F2].
